executive_assessment.text: Nigeria has substantial and geographically differentiated physical climate risk, but climate-FCV evidence is much narrower than the physical-risk evidence.
The best-supported Climate-FCV mechanisms operate through livelihoods, mobility, land/resource governance, displacement and service access - not direct climate -> violence causation.
Nigeria has formal climate and disaster institutions and demonstrable project outputs, but implementation, local-level capacity, M&E and independently verified outcomes remain material constraints.

coverage.value: Heat, rainfall variability, drought, flood and coastal/SLR risks are documented.
coverage.gap_note: Accessible projections rely substantially on 2021/CMIP5 evidence; newer scenario detail needs verification.

coverage.value: National flood exposure and selected NE/Lagos/local compound events are documented.
coverage.gap_note: Coastal-city exposure beyond Lagos and recent state-level comparative exposure remain thin.

coverage.value: Agriculture, pastoral livelihoods, displaced people, children and women show differentiated sensitivity.
coverage.gap_note: Household-level and gender-disaggregated national evidence is incomplete.

coverage.value: Humanitarian delivery and anticipatory flood systems are documented.
coverage.gap_note: Household coping and informal/community coping capacity are weakly evaluated.

coverage.value: NAP architecture, watershed agencies and community groups provide capacity evidence.
coverage.gap_note: Operational effectiveness across states/LGAs is unevenly documented.

coverage.value: Multi-tier institutional architecture exists but coordination, skills, finance and M&E gaps persist.
coverage.gap_note: Evidence is stronger on formal structures than implementation results.

coverage.value: Independent IEG review provides outcome/output evidence for NEWMAP.
coverage.gap_note: Few other current climate/DRM programmes have independent outcome evidence in this packet.

coverage.value: Pastoral mobility/governance and Lake Chad FCV -> vulnerability mechanisms are documented.
coverage.gap_note: Evidence is geographically clustered and causal certainty remains limited.

coverage.value: Livelihood resilience and governance are plausible peace-supporting capacities.
coverage.gap_note: Direct evidence that adaptation/DRR interventions reduced violence is absent.

coverage.value: All listed pressure families have traceable evidence.
coverage.gap_note: Current CMIP6 page-level projections remain a gap.

coverage.value: Agriculture/pastoralism/water and urban flooding are strongest; fisheries/energy are covered more thinly.
coverage.gap_note: Energy/fisheries need more current sector-specific analysis.

coverage.value: Mobility, displacement and farmer-herder mechanisms are well represented; inequality evidence is thinner.
Insecurity and service/access effects are strong; pollution is deliberately not relabelled climate impact.
coverage.gap_note: Market-price pathways and Niger Delta pollution/climate interactions are thin.

coverage.value: Federal/state/local formal capacity documented; customary and pastoral institutions less well evidenced.
coverage.gap_note: Customary dispute-resolution and pastoral institutions need targeted sources.

coverage.value: One independent climate-resilience project review is included.
coverage.gap_note: Major gap for current programmes, livestock reform, anticipatory action and peacebuilding.

geographic_notes.text: National physical-climate evidence should not be used to erase Nigeria's ecological and FCV differences. The accessible evidence distinguishes arid/semi-arid northern settings, the Middle Belt pastoral-farming interface, the Northeast/Lake Chad conflict and displacement context, and Lagos/coastal exposure. (UNFCCC1)

The Middle Belt farmer-herder evidence is subnational, and its mechanisms should not be projected onto the Niger Delta, Lagos, the Southeast or the entire North. Likewise, the 2026 Surulere flood assessment is evidence about six Lagos communities, not Nigerian urban flooding in general.

The Northeast combines insurgency-related displacement, humanitarian-access constraints, food insecurity and flood exposure. Northwest and North Central displacement have distinct conflict patterns and should not be subsumed under the Northeast insurgency model.

The Niger Delta/coastal zone is physically exposed to sea-level rise, inundation and erosion, but oil spills, pollution, gas flaring, sand mining and infrastructure-driven coastal change must remain distinct unless a source establishes a climate interaction. The Adaptation Communication itself recognizes several of these anthropogenic non-climate contributors. (UNFCCC1)

Important underrepresented areas include much of the Southeast, Northwest beyond displacement aggregates, smaller coastal settlements outside Lagos/Niger Delta, and state/local contexts without recent humanitarian or project evidence.

sector_notes.text: *Relatively well covered: agriculture and pastoralism; water/watersheds; disaster management; food/nutrition; humanitarian logistics; displacement; urban flooding; climate governance.

*Thinner: fisheries, energy/hydropower, coastal infrastructure performance, health beyond nutrition, land-tenure administration, informal/customary conflict resolution, market-price transmission, Niger Delta climate-pollution interaction, and evaluated urban adaptation.

known_gaps.text: Climate projections: the best page-verified national projection source available here is the 2021 Adaptation Communication using CMIP5/RCP8.5. A World Bank Climate Risk Country Profile surfaced in search but its PDF returned a 403 when opened, while the 2026 CCDR PDF could not be checked page by page. The newer physical-risk baseline therefore remains incomplete.
Geographic/population gaps: farmer-herder and Lake Chad findings are geographically specific; evidence is too thin to build comparable pathways for every geopolitical zone.

Evaluation gaps: independent outcome evaluation is available for NEWMAP, but not in this packet for the 2026 anticipatory flood mechanism, recent livestock reforms, community peacebuilding, NAP implementation, or Lagos/coastal adaptation.

Unintended effects: IEG's NEWMAP review has a section for unintended impacts but records no assessed unintended impact there; broader maladaptation and distributional effects remain weakly evaluated. (World Bank3)
Differentiated vulnerability: the Adaptation Communication itself reports gaps in sex-disaggregated/resource-control data and limited documentation of Indigenous/traditional participation.

Causal uncertainty: the climate -> farmer/herder-conflict pathway has meaningful evidence but cannot isolate climate from land governance, agricultural expansion, arms, criminality, politics, identity and historical relations.

FCV -> climate/adaptation direction: evidence exists for Lake Chad livelihood restrictions and contemporary humanitarian-access constraints, but nationwide causal evidence on how insecurity changes adaptation outcomes is weak.

Food-security attribution: current WFP and IPC evidence strongly documents conflict, access, displacement, disease, weak health systems and funding constraints. Climate should not be inserted as a proximate driver where those current analyses do not establish it. (World Food Programme8)
Coastal attribution: sea-level rise is relevant, but specific erosion/flood losses can also depend heavily on drainage, jetties, sand mining, land-use planning, infrastructure and maintenance.

Access limitations: official Nigeria-hosted copies of the 2021 NDC and climate-policy PDFs returned gateway errors during verification; the UNFCCC-hosted Adaptation Communication and NDC registry were used instead.
